cards.explanation: The answer is leaping across the mountains. She says, “Listen! My beloved approaches. Look! Here he comes, leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills.” Mountains, friends. I get winded hopping over a bag of flour. Her beloved treats a whole mountain range like a speed bump.

The answer is that he calls her to arise and come away with him. He calls to her, “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one.” He isn't asking her to stay put. He wants her up and out the door with him.

The answer is the season of singing. He says, “The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land.” Winter's over, the rain's gone, and the whole countryside is warming up its voice. I think even the turtledoves are showing off a little.

The answer is False. He says, “The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance.” The tree is busy ripening figs, and the vines are blossoming. Winter is over and everything is waking up.
The answer is True. The voice says, “…let me see your face, let me hear your voice…” He asks for both, her face and her voice. He adds, “for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is lovely.”

The answer is False. The text says, “Catch for us the foxes—the little foxes that ruin the vineyards—for our vineyards are in bloom.” The reason it gives is that the vineyards are in bloom, not that they're already ruined.

The answer is that she and her beloved belong to each other. She says, “My beloved is mine and I am his…” Short, sweet and no wasted words, friends. Then she adds that he “…pastures his flock among the lilies.”

The answer is before the day breaks. She says, “Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of Bether.” The clock is the sunrise. Mountains of Bether is a place named right there in her song. I think she wants every minute before the light comes.
The answer is False. She says, “I sought him, but did not find him.” She's on her bed at night, looking, and she doesn't find him. I think that's a long, quiet kind of night.

The answer is that she gets up and searches the city. She says, “I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares. I will seek the one I love.” She doesn't wait around. The search moves out into the streets and squares.

The answer is the watchmen. She says, “I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city…” They were out on their rounds, and she ran into them. Watchmen, out in the city at night, and she meets them.
The word is seen. She asks, “Have you seen the one I love?” It's a simple question, friends. She's out in the city at night, and the watchmen are who she asks.
The answer is True. She says, “I had just passed them when I found the one I love.” She asked the watchmen, moved on, and found him. All that searching and there he is.

The answer is her mother's house. She says, “I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother’s house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me.” She holds on until she's brought him there. That's some determination.

The answer is not to awaken love until the time is right. She says, “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.” It's a solemn charge, and she means it. Love has a right time, and she asks them to wait for it.
